All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give a single exact real number equal to the infimum of all c in [0,1] for which the stated finite triangle-free homomorphism-target property holds, and justify that it is the infimum. It need not decide whether the property holds at the infimum itself.

A team of 4 agents was told that the answer is \frac{1}{9} and asked to prove it (its two halves: Proving \(1/9\) takes two halves: for every \(c\in(1/9,1]\), there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that every graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), with every vertex having at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\); and for every \(c\in[0,1/9)\) and every finite graph \(H\) containing no cycle of length \(3\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\) and a graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), with every vertex having at least \(cn\) neighbors, that admits no homomorphism to \(H\).), writing Python that checks every step. Their run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. The answer they were told may be wrong: teams told a wrong answer sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof anyway. Their whole record is in your folder, read-only:

7	We prove both directions. The upper bound uses a regularity argument; the lower bound uses an elementary shift-graph construction. In particular, no theorem about Kneser graphs is needed.
8	
9	## 1. Preliminary observations
10	
11	For a graph \(G\), let \(J(G)\) be the graph on \(V(G)\) in which distinct vertices are adjacent if they are joined in \(G\) by a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\).
12	
13	Suppose \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\). Then
14	\[
15	xy\in E(J(G))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_G(x)\cap N_G(y)=\varnothing. \tag{1}
16	\]
17	Indeed, a common neighbor, together with the odd walk, would give a closed odd walk of length \(3\) or \(5\). Every closed odd walk contains an odd cycle of no greater length.
18	
19	### A bounded coloring of \(J(G)\) gives a finite triangle-free target
20	
21	For a positive integer \(q\), define \(W_q\) as follows:
22	\[
23	V(W_q)=\{(i,A):i\in[q],\ A\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\}\}.
24	\]
25	Join \((i,A)\) and \((j,B)\) exactly when
26	\[
27	i\in B,\qquad j\in A,\qquad A\cap B=\varnothing. \tag{2}
28	\]
29	
30	This graph is triangle-free: in a supposed triangle, the first coordinate of the third vertex would belong to both sets attached to the first two vertices, contrary to (2).
31	
32	If \(\gamma\) is a proper \(q\)-coloring of \(J(G)\), then
33	\[
34	v\longmapsto \bigl(\gamma(v),\{\gamma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}\bigr) \tag{3}
35	\]
36	is a homomorphism \(G\to W_q\). For an edge \(xy\), the two neighbor-color sets are disjoint: a shared color would give equally colored endpoints of a length-three walk through \(xy\). Thus (2) holds.
37	
38	Consequently, for the upper bound it is enough to bound \(\chi(J(G))\).
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 2. The upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
43	
44	Fix \(c>1/9\), and put
45	\[
46	t=\frac{9c-1}{1000},\qquad \varepsilon=t^2.
47	\]
48	Thus \(0<t\le 0.008\).
49	
50	We use the equitable regularity lemma in the following form.
51	
52	### Regularity lemma
53	
54	For every \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\) and integer \(m_0\), there is \(K\) such that every sufficiently large graph has a partition
55	\[
56	V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_\ell
57	\]
58	where
59	\[
60	|V_0|\le\varepsilon n,\qquad
61	m_0\le\ell\le K,\qquad
62	|V_1|=\cdots=|V_\ell|,
63	\]
64	and at most \(\varepsilon\ell^2\) unordered cluster pairs are not \(\varepsilon\)-regular.
65	
66	Here a pair \((A,B)\), of density \(d(A,B)\), is \(\varepsilon\)-regular if every \(A'\subseteq A,B'\subseteq B\) with \(|A'|\ge\varepsilon|A|\), \(|B'|\ge\varepsilon|B|\) satisfies
67	\[
68	|d(A',B')-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon.
69	\]
70	
71	For completeness, an energy proof is given in Section 4.
72	
73	### 2.1. The reduced graph and neighborhood profiles
74	
75	Apply the lemma with \(m_0\ge1/\varepsilon\). We may assume \(n\) is sufficiently large that the common cluster size \(m\) satisfies
76	\[
77	m\ge \frac{20}{t^2}. \tag{4}
78	\]
79	
80	Discard every cluster incident with more than \(t\ell\) irregular pairs. There are at most \(2t\ell\) discarded clusters. Put them into the exceptional set \(E\), so
81	\[
82	|E|\le(\varepsilon+2t)n.
83	\]
84	Let \(k\) be the number of remaining clusters.
85	
86	Define a reduced graph \(R\) on these clusters: a pair is an edge if it is \(\varepsilon\)-regular and has density at least \(t\).
87	
88	Averaging the original minimum-degree condition over a remaining cluster gives
89	\[
90	d_R(i)m\ge (c-4t-2\varepsilon)n.
91	\]
92	To see the error terms, neighbors in \(E\) cost at most \((\varepsilon+2t)n\); neighbors in the same cluster cost at most \(\varepsilon n\); irregular pairs cost at most \(tn\); and regular pairs of density below \(t\) cost at most \(tn\). Therefore
93	\[
94	\delta(R)\ge(c-6t)k>0. \tag{5}
95	\]
96	
97	For every vertex \(v\), including vertices in \(E\), define its profile
98	\[
99	S(v)=\{i:|N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge tm\}.
100	\]
101	Outside the clusters indexed by \(S(v)\), the vertex has at most
102	\[
103	|E|+tkm\le4tn
104	\]
105	neighbors. Hence
106	\[
107	|S(v)|\ge(c-4t)k>0. \tag{6}
108	\]
109	
110	Call a profile \(S\) **bad** if its profile class contains an edge of \(J(G)\). By (1), the endpoints of that edge have disjoint neighborhoods. Almost all those neighborhoods lie in the clusters of \(S\), so
111	\[
112	|S|m\ge2(c-4t)n,
113	\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad
114	|S|\ge2(c-4t)k. \tag{7}
115	\]
116	
117	### 2.2. Three consequences of regularity
118	
119	Write \(N_R(S)=\bigcup_{i\in S}N_R(i)\). We need:
120	
121	1. **Every \(S(v)\) is independent in \(R\).**
122	
123	   Otherwise a regular edge between two clusters of \(S(v)\) supplies an edge between their large subsets of neighbors of \(v\), making a triangle.
124	
125	2. **If \(xy\in E(G)\), then**
126	   \[
127	   N_R(S(x))\cap N_R(S(y))=\varnothing. \tag{8}
128	   \]
129	
130	   Otherwise there are \(i\in S(x)\), \(j\in S(y)\), and a cluster \(h\) with \(ih,jh\in E(R)\). Regularity supplies a path
131	   \[
132	   x-a-b-d-y
133	   \]
134	   with \(a\in V_i,b\in V_h,d\in V_j\). Together with \(xy\), this is a \(C_5\).
135	
136	   This also works when \(i=j\): almost every vertex of \(V_h\) has many neighbors in each of the two large endpoint subsets, and distinct endpoints can be chosen.
137	
138	3. **If \(x-z-y\) is a length-two path, then there is no \(R\)-edge between \(S(x)\) and \(S(y)\).**
139	
140	   Such an edge would supply a path \(x-a-b-y\), which, together with \(x-z-y\), makes a \(C_5\).
141	
142	These applications produce genuine cycles, not merely closed walks. Here are the quantitative details. Delete the at most three prescribed original vertices from each endpoint subset. Its remaining size is at least \(tm-3>\varepsilon m\). A regular pair of density at least \(t\) connects two such subsets. Moreover, all but \(\varepsilon m\) vertices on the other side have at least
143	\[
144	(t-\varepsilon)(tm-3)>3
145	\]
146	neighbors in a given endpoint subset. Thus a common central vertex and distinct endpoints can be chosen while avoiding the prescribed vertices. Inequality (4) ensures all these bounds.
147	
148	By (5) and (8),
149	\[
150	xy\in E(G)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(x)\cap S(y)=\varnothing: \tag{9}
151	\]
152	a common cluster would have a neighbor in \(R\), contradicting (8). In particular, each profile class is independent in \(G\).
153	
154	### 2.3. A high chromatic number would force nine units of degree mass
155	
156	There are at most
157	\[
158	M=2^k
159	\]
160	profiles. Fix one profile class \(P\).
161	
162	For every edge \(xy\) of \(J(G)[P]\), choose and orient a witnessing path
163	\[
164	x-a-b-y.
165	\]
166	Such a simple length-three path exists because \(P\) is independent in \(G\). Color the oriented edge by the ordered pair of profiles of \(a,b\). There are at most \(M^2\) edge colors.
167	
168	If every one-color subgraph were bipartite, the product of their two-colorings would give
169	\[
170	\chi(J(G)[P])\le2^{M^2}.
171	\]
172	Otherwise, a nonbipartite one-color subgraph has a directed two-edge path: an orientation without such a path has every nonisolated vertex either a source or a sink and is therefore bipartite.
173	
174	The two witnesses concatenate to
175	\[
176	x_0-a_0-b_0-x_1-a_1-b_1-x_2, \tag{10}
177	\]
178	whose profiles are
179	\[
180	p,q,r,p,q,r,p.
181	\]
182	The three profiles are distinct by (9). Also \(a_0\ne a_1\) and \(b_0\ne b_1\), since either equality would create a triangle. Thus (10) shows that all three profiles \(p,q,r\) are bad.
183	
184	Put
185	\[
186	S_1=p,\quad S_2=q,\quad S_3=r,\qquad T_i=N_R(S_i).
187	\]
188	These six sets are pairwise disjoint:
189	
190	- Actual \(G\)-edges occur between every pair of the three profiles, so (8) makes the \(T_i\) pairwise disjoint, and (9) makes the \(S_i\) pairwise disjoint.
191	- The path (10) contains length-two paths between every pair of profile types. Consequence 3 prohibits every \(R\)-edge between different \(S_i\).
192	- Consequence 1 prohibits edges inside each \(S_i\).
193	
194	The last two facts say that every \(S_i\) is disjoint from every \(T_j\).
195	
196	By (7), each \(S_i\) has size at least \(2(c-4t)k\). By (5), each nonempty \(S_i\) has
197	\[
198	|T_i|\ge(c-6t)k.
199	\]
200	Consequently,
201	\[
202	\begin{aligned}
203	k
204	&\ge\sum_{i=1}^3(|S_i|+|T_i|)\\
205	&\ge\bigl(6(c-4t)+3(c-6t)\bigr)k\\
206	&=(9c-42t)k>k,
207	\end{aligned}
208	\]
209	because
210	\[
211	9c-42t-1=\frac{958}{1000}(9c-1)>0.
212	\]
213	This is impossible.
214	
215	It follows that
216	\[
217	\chi(J(G))\le M\,2^{M^2}.
218	\]
219	Since \(k\le K\), this is a bound depending only on \(c\).
220	
221	By (3), all sufficiently large graphs in question map to one fixed triangle-free \(W_q\). For the finitely many smaller orders, take a disjoint copy of every \(C_3,C_5\)-free graph of those orders and add them to \(W_q\). This gives the required finite triangle-free graph \(H_c\).
222	
223	Thus every \(c>1/9\) has the stated property.
224	
225	---
226	
227	## 3. The lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails
228	
229	Fix \(c<1/9\) and a finite triangle-free graph \(H\). An empty \(H\) is immediate, so assume \(h=|V(H)|\ge1\).
230	
231	### 3.1. High-chromatic shift graphs with an almost-half independent cover
232	
233	For \(N\ge k\), the shift graph \(S(N,k)\) has the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([N]\) as vertices. Its edges join
234	\[
235	(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\quad\text{and}\quad(x_2,\ldots,x_{k+1})
236	\]
237	for each increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple.
238	
239	For fixed \(k\), its chromatic number tends to infinity with \(N\). Here is an elementary proof.
240	
241	If \(S(N,j)\) has a \(q\)-coloring \(f\), color a \((j-1)\)-tuple \(z\) by the set
242	\[
243	C(z)=\{f(z,t):t>\max z\}.
244	\]
245	This is a proper coloring with at most \(2^q\) colors. Indeed, for adjacent
246	\[
247	z=(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}),\qquad z'=(x_2,\ldots,x_j),
248	\]
249	the color \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_j)\) belongs to \(C(z)\) but cannot belong to \(C(z')\), since that would give equally colored adjacent \(j\)-tuples. Empty extension sets cause no problem.
250	
251	Iteration reaches \(S(N,1)=K_N\). Thus, defining
252	\[
253	T_0(q)=q,\qquad T_{s+1}(q)=2^{T_s(q)},
254	\]
255	a \(q\)-coloring of \(S(N,k)\) implies
256	\[
257	N\le T_{k-1}(q). \tag{11}
258	\]
259	
260	Now let \(k\ge3\) be odd. For each permutation \(\pi\) of \([N]\), let \(I_\pi\) consist of the \(k\)-tuples whose \(\pi\)-largest entry occurs in an even position.
261	
262	Each \(I_\pi\) is independent. For two adjacent tuples, if the largest entry in their union is an end entry, its position in its tuple is \(1\) or \(k\), both odd. Otherwise its two positions differ by one, so both cannot be even.
263	
264	Every tuple belongs to exactly
265	\[
266	p=\frac{k-1}{2k}N!
267	\]
268	of these independent sets. Put \(m=N!\), and, for each vertex \(u\), write
269	\[
270	I_u=\{\pi:u\in I_\pi\}.
271	\]
272	Then
273	\[
274	|I_u|=p,\qquad uv\in E(S(N,k))\Longrightarrow I_u\cap I_v=\varnothing. \tag{12}
275	\]
276	
277	Choose odd \(k\) sufficiently large that
278	\[
279	\frac{p}{3(m+p)}
280	=\frac{k-1}{3(3k-1)}>c. \tag{13}
281	\]
282	Next choose \(N>T_{k-1}(h)\). By (11), the graph
283	\[
284	F=S(N,k)
285	\]
286	has chromatic number greater than \(h\).
287	
288	### 3.2. The dense graph
289	
290	Orient \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace each oriented edge \(u\to v\) by
291	\[
292	u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v,
293	\]
294	obtaining a graph \(X\). Give its vertices types and labels:
295	\[
296	\begin{array}{c|ccc}
297	\text{vertex}&u&a_{uv}&b_{uv}\\ \hline
298	\text{type}&0&1&2\\
299	\text{label}&u&u&v .
300	\end{array}
301	\]
302	
303	We use this elementary local fact:
304	
305	> Endpoints of a length-three walk in \(X\) having the same type have adjacent labels in \(F\).
306	
307	For type \(0\), the walk traverses a subdivided edge. For type \(1\), the possible forms are
308	\[
309	a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v-a_{vw},
310	\qquad
311	a_{uv}-u-b_{wu}-a_{wu},
312	\]
313	whose endpoint labels are respectively \(u,v\) and \(u,w\). Type \(2\) is symmetric.
314	
315	For an integer \(L\ge1\), add three disjoint complete bipartite graphs with sides
316	\[
317	P_i=[m]\times[L],\qquad |Q_i|=pL,\qquad i=0,1,2.
318	\]
319	Identify \([m]\) with the permutations of \([N]\). For a vertex \(x\in X\) of type \(i\) and label \(u\), join \(x\) to every
320	\[
321	(\pi,\ell)\in P_i\quad\text{with }\pi\in I_u.
322	\]
323	Call the resulting graph \(G\).
324	
325	Its order and minimum degree satisfy
326	\[
327	n=|X|+3(m+p)L,\qquad \delta(G)\ge pL. \tag{14}
328	\]
329	Every \(X\)-vertex has \(pL\) attachments; every \(P_i\)-vertex has \(pL\) neighbors in \(Q_i\); and every \(Q_i\)-vertex has \(mL\ge pL\) neighbors.
330	
331	By (13), sufficiently large \(L\) makes \(pL\ge cn\).
332	
333	### 3.3. No triangles and no \(5\)-cycles
334	
335	The graph \(X\) has girth at least \(9\): every cycle traverses complete three-edge subdivisions of edges of the simple graph \(F\).
336	
337	No triangle or \(5\)-cycle contains a vertex of \(Q_i\). Its two cycle neighbors would lie in \(P_i\), with an alternative path of length \(1\) or \(3\) between them. Length \(1\) is impossible. For length \(3\), both interior vertices lie in \(Q_i\cup X_i\), which is independent.
338	
339	Now consider cycles avoiding all \(Q_i\).
340	
341	- A triangle containing a \(P_i\)-vertex would require an \(X\)-edge between vertices of the same type, impossible.
342	- A \(5\)-cycle with exactly one \(P_i\)-vertex would contain a length-three \(X\)-path whose same-type endpoints share a permutation in their label sets. The local fact and (12) forbid this.
343	- A \(5\)-cycle with two \(P\)-vertices has one arc containing just one \(X\)-vertex. That forces both \(P\)-vertices into the same pool. The other arc then contains an \(X\)-edge within one type, impossible.
344	- More than two \(P\)-vertices cannot occur in a \(5\)-cycle because their union is independent.
345	
346	Thus \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).
347	
348	### 3.4. No homomorphism to \(H\)
349	
350	Suppose \(G\to H\). The images of the original vertices of \(F\) give a proper \(h\)-coloring of \(F\): endpoints of an edge of \(F\) are joined by a length-three path in \(X\), and their images cannot coincide, since a closed length-three walk in a simple graph is a triangle.
351	
352	This contradicts \(\chi(F)>h\).
353	
354	Therefore every \(c<1/9\) fails. Together with Section 2, this proves the claimed infimum.
355	
356	---
357	
358	## 4. Energy proof of the regularity lemma used above
359	
360	Here are the details to make the upper argument independent of a regularity black box.
361	
362	For a partition \(\mathcal P\), define its energy by
363	\[
364	\mathcal E(\mathcal P)=
365	\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}\frac{|A||B|}{n^2}d(A,B)^2.
366	\]
367	Regard every exceptional vertex as a singleton part. Then \(0\le\mathcal E\le1\), and refinement never decreases energy, by the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
368	
369	Start with \(m_0\) equal main clusters and fewer than \(m_0\) exceptional vertices. For sufficiently large \(n\), the exception has size at most \(\varepsilon n/2\).
370	
371	If there are more than \(\varepsilon\ell^2\) irregular main-cluster pairs, choose witness subsets for each pair and split each cluster by all witnesses involving it. There are at most \(2^\ell\) resulting atoms per cluster.
372	
373	For one irregular pair, its witness rectangle has relative weight at least \(\varepsilon^2\) and density differing from the old density by more than \(\varepsilon\). Its two ordered energy contributions therefore increase by at least
374	\[
375	2\varepsilon^4m^2/n^2.
376	\]
377	Summed over the irregular pairs, the increase is greater than
378	\[
379	2\varepsilon^5(\ell m/n)^2\ge\varepsilon^5,
380	\]
381	provided the exceptional set has size at most \(\varepsilon n\).
382	
383	Let \(T=\lceil2\varepsilon^{-5}\rceil\). After splitting, equitize inside the atoms into blocks of size
384	\[
385	s=\left\lfloor\frac{\varepsilon n}{2T\ell2^\ell}\right\rfloor.
386	\]
387	Make every leftover vertex an exceptional singleton. This is still a refinement, so no energy is lost. At most
388	\[
389	\ell2^\ell s\le\frac{\varepsilon n}{2T}
390	\]
391	new vertices become exceptional per step.
392	
393	If \(s\ge1\), the new number of clusters is at most
394	\[
395	\frac{4T\ell2^\ell}{\varepsilon}.
396	\]
397	Every old cluster retains at least one block, so the number remains at least \(m_0\). If \(s=0\), use the all-singleton partition; then
398	\[
399	n<\frac{2T\ell2^\ell}{\varepsilon},
400	\]
401	so its number of clusters is bounded as well.
402	
403	There cannot be \(T\) energy-increasing failures, since energy is at most \(1\). The exceptional set remains at most
404	\[
405	\varepsilon n/2+T\cdot\varepsilon n/(2T)=\varepsilon n.
406	\]
407	The displayed recurrence bounds the final number of clusters solely in terms of \(\varepsilon,m_0\), proving the lemma.
408	
409	---

411	## 5. Runnable exact finite checks
412	
413	The mathematical arguments above establish the statements for all parameters. The following standalone Python checks actual constructions and the finite structural assertions, rather than printing assumed answers.
414	
415	It uses Python 3 and NumPy. It:
416	
417	- constructs shift graphs and their permutation covers;
418	- checks every cover size and every edge-disjointness condition;
419	- constructs the augmented lower-bound graphs;
420	- checks minimum degree and exact counts of closed walks of lengths \(3,5\);
421	- checks the color-set descent;
422	- constructs the universal targets and checks triangles;
423	- exhausts all reduced graphs on six vertices and every admissible assignment of three supports, including overlapping assignments.
424	
425	```python
426	from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
427	from math import factorial
428	import numpy as np
429	
430	
431	def shift_instance(N, k):
432	    assert N >= k >= 3 and k % 2 == 1
433	
434	    vertices = list(combinations(range(N), k))
